content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 226 of the Constitution of India is titled “Power of High Courts to issue certain writs”. It forms an integral component of The States (Articles 152–237), located within the “High Courts” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 32 3 [omitted , every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

(2) The power conferred by clause (1) to issue directions, orders or writs to any Government, authority or person may also be exercised by any High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises for the exercise of such power, and subsequently ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 29 . . 226A" omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 7 . beginning with "writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them" and ending with "such illegality has resulted in substantial failure of justice." . notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories. (3) Where any party against whom an interim order, whether by way of injunction or stay or in any other manner, is made on, or in any proceedings relating to, a petition under clause (1), without—

(a) furnishing to such party copies of such petition and all documents in support of the plea for such interim order; and

(b) giving such party an opportunity of being heard, makes an application to the High Court for the vacation of such order and furnishes a copy of such application to the party in whose favour such order has been made or the counsel of such party, the High Court shall dispose of the application within a period of two weeks from the date on which it is received or from the date on which the copy of such application is so furnished, whichever is later, or where the High Court is closed on the last day of that period, before the expiry of the next day afterwards on which the High Court is open; and if the application is not so disposed of, the interim order shall, on the expiry of that period, or, as the case may be, the expiry of the said next day, stand vacated. (4) The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 226 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. Key aspect: Wider than Article 32: “for any other purpose” covers non-fundamental legal rights. Territorial reach is the cause of action, not only the seat of the authority.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: Extraordinary original constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court (Art. 226) or Supreme Court (Art. 32). High Court jurisdiction extends to Fundamental Rights and “for any other purpose”.
2. Standard of Review: Judicial review of administrative, quasi-judicial, and legislative action on grounds of illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety, or manifest arbitrariness.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved person for personal prerogative relief; expanded standing / PIL for public duty enforcement and marginalized groups.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish

(3) Where any party against whom an interim order, whether by way of injunction or stay or in any other manner, is made on, or in any proceedings relating to, a petition under clause (1), without—
3. (a) furnishing to such party copies of such petition and all documents in support of the plea for such interim order; and
4. (b) giving such party an opportunity of being heard, makes an application to the High Court for the vacation of such order and furnishes a copy of such application to the party in whose favour such order has been made or the counsel of such party, the High Court shall dispose of the application within a period of two weeks from the date on which it is received or from the date on which the copy of such application is so furnished, whichever is later, or where the High Court is closed on the last day of that period, before the expiry of the next day afterwards on which the High Court is open; and if the application is not so disposed of, the interim order shall, on the expiry of that period, or, as the case may be, the expiry of the said next day, stand vacated. (4) The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 226 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Direct Application (Constitutional Guarantee / Power Upheld)
examples.body: State action or statutory exercise strictly satisfies the conditions laid down under Article 226 (Power of High Courts to issue certain writs). The authority acts within constitutional bounds, respects procedural fairness, and advances the constitutional objective of High Courts. Outcome: Action is held valid and enforceable by the Court.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Condition / Breach (State Action Fails)
examples.body: An executive order or legislation violates or bypasses the express procedural conditions, jurisdictional threshold, or fundamental guarantees of Article 226. The action is tainted by manifest arbitrariness, lacks legislative competence, or ignores mandatory safeguards. Outcome: The Court strikes down the measure or issues a writ of certiorari / mandamus.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the impugned directive in light of Article 226 and settled Supreme Court jurisprudence. What relief, if any, can be granted?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 226 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 226.
3. Examine procedural compliance: Substantive and procedural requirements under the Constitution cannot be waived on mere grounds of administrative convenience.
4. Balance public interest vs constitutional discipline: Constitutional limitations always prevail over executive fiat.

misconceptions.trap: Treating Article 226 as a standalone provision divorced from the rest of the Constitution.
misconceptions.correction: The Constitution is an organic whole. Article 226 must be interpreted harmoniously with Part III Fundamental Rights, the Preamble, and basic structure doctrine.

misconceptions.trap: Writing only the article heading without deconstructing constitutional ingredients, procedural anchors, and landmark ratios.
misconceptions.correction: A comprehensive legal analysis requires full IRAC structure: statutory anatomy, proving ingredients, procedural forum, leading case ratio, and practical application.

misconceptions.trap: Confusing the scope of Article 32 (only Part III FRs) with Article 226 (FRs and any other purpose).
misconceptions.correction: Verify whether Article 226 falls in Part III or another Part before advising the choice of writ forum. Article 32 cannot be moved for non-Part III rights unless connected to a Fundamental Right breach.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 226 (Power of High Courts to issue certain writs)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 226 (Power of High Courts to issue certain writs) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 226 is situated in The States (Articles 152–237), governing the “High Courts” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) Notwithstanding anything in article 32 3 [omitted , every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
2. (2) The power conferred by clause (1) to issue directions, orders or writs to any Government, authority or person may also be exercised by any High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises for the exercise of such power, and subsequently ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 29 . . 226A" omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 7 . beginning with "writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them" and ending with "such illegality has resulted in substantial failure of justice." . notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories. (3) Where any party against whom an interim order, whether by way of injunction or stay or in any other manner, is made on, or in any proceedings relating to, a petition under clause (1), without—
3. (a) furnishing to such party copies of such petition and all documents in support of the plea for such interim order; and
4. (b) giving such party an opportunity of being heard, makes an application to the High Court for the vacation of such order and furnishes a copy of such application to the party in whose favour such order has been made or the counsel of such party, the High Court shall dispose of the application within a period of two weeks from the date on which it is received or from the date on which the copy of such application is so furnished, whichever is later, or where the High Court is closed on the last day of that period, before the expiry of the next day afterwards on which the High Court is open; and if the application is not so disposed of, the interim order shall, on the expiry of that period, or, as the case may be, the expiry of the said next day, stand vacated. (4) The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: Extraordinary original constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court (Art. 226) or Supreme Court (Art. 32). High Court jurisdiction extends to Fundamental Rights and “for any other purpose”.
2. Standard of Review: Judicial review of administrative, quasi-judicial, and legislative action on grounds of illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety, or manifest arbitrariness.
3. Standing: Aggrieved person for personal prerogative relief; expanded standing / PIL for public duty enforcement and marginalized groups.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 226:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 226 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.question: Comprehensive Constitutional Written Submissions: Doctrinal Scheme & Judicial Evolution of Article 226 (Power of High Courts to issue certain writs)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 226 of the Constitution of India, titled “Power of High Courts to issue certain writs”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The States (Articles 152–237), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 226 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) Notwithstanding anything in article 32 3 [omitted , every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
(a) Limb 2: (2) The power conferred by clause (1) to issue directions, orders or writs to any Government, authority or person may also be exercised by any High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises for the exercise of such power, and subsequently ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 29 . . 226A" omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 7 . beginning with "writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them" and ending with "such illegality has resulted in substantial failure of justice." . notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories. (3) Where any party against whom an interim order, whether by way of injunction or stay or in any other manner, is made on, or in any proceedings relating to, a petition under clause (1), without—
(a) Limb 3: (a) furnishing to such party copies of such petition and all documents in support of the plea for such interim order; and
(a) Limb 4: (b) giving such party an opportunity of being heard, makes an application to the High Court for the vacation of such order and furnishes a copy of such application to the party in whose favour such order has been made or the counsel of such party, the High Court shall dispose of the application within a period of two weeks from the date on which it is received or from the date on which the copy of such application is so furnished, whichever is later, or where the High Court is closed on the last day of that period, before the expiry of the next day afterwards on which the High Court is open; and if the application is not so disposed of, the interim order shall, on the expiry of that period, or, as the case may be, the expiry of the said next day, stand vacated. (4) The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 226 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 226 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 226:
1. Forum Selection: Extraordinary original constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court (Art. 226) or Supreme Court (Art. 32). High Court jurisdiction extends to Fundamental Rights and “for any other purpose”.
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 226;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 226 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 226?
Rule: Under Article 226, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 226 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.
